canberra.title: Crossbench MPs and senators push Red Lines package on human rights
canberra.snippet: Much of the crossbench in both houses of parliament is uniting this week to put the hard word on Labor over human rights. Specifically, i...
canberra.content:
ACT independent Senator David Pocock is among the crossbenchers from both houses of parliament sponsoring the Red Lines bill on human rights. Photo: Region.

Much of the crossbench in both houses of parliament is uniting this week to put the hard word on Labor over human rights.

Specifically, independents and Greens are jointly presenting a package of private members’ bills to upgrade Australia’s domestic legislation to bring it into line with international obligations.

More pointedly, the group is hoping to put pressure on the Federal Government to ban Australian goods from being used by the Israeli military.

This would include Australian-manufactured parts for F-35 fighter jets.

The move is necessary, they say, because Australia lacks a federal Human Rights Act.

The bills would outlaw everything from defence equipment and technology to services if they could be used in breach of Australia’s international human rights obligations.

The package, the group has labelled Red Lines, was set to be introduced in the House of Representatives on Monday (14 September) by independent Member for Mackellar, Sophie Scamps, and seconded by the independent Member for Clark, Andrew Wilkie.

At the same time, it is co-sponsored in the Upper House by independent senators David Pocock, Lidia Thorpe and Fatima Payman, as well as Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi.

On Tuesday evening, former Human Rights Commissioner Gillian Triggs will officially launch the reform package at a special Parliament House event.

The crossbenchers say their suite of legislative amendments has “huge support across civil society” and shifts the focus from prohibition to prevention.

“Of all the many issues people contact me about, human rights and the Gaza genocide is by far the biggest,” Senator Pocock said.

“I have received thousands of emails from Canberrans desperately concerned about the indiscriminate killing we have seen overseas.

“At the same time we know there is huge support for a federal human rights act and legislation that will give effect in our domestic laws to the obligations we have signed up to in international treaties and conventions. This package of bills is sensible ”

The Red Lines omnibus bill seeks to strengthen Australian law to ensure the nation’s government, companies and institutions do not in any way contribute to genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity or illegal occupation.

It would reform defence exports, investment, corporate accountability and trade.

The bill seeks to stop Australian defence goods, technology and services being supplied where there is a real risk they could enable genocide, war crimes or crimes against humanity, and require greater transparency and oversight of defence exports.

It would also stop the Future Fund, super funds and registered charities investing in companies or activities connected to illegal settlements or serious violations of international law, and require divestment where such investments are identified.

The package includes an accountability factor, requiring large companies, defence-related businesses, Commonwealth entities and other covered organisations to identify and report on genocide risks in their operations and supply chains.

It also bans the import and sale of goods produced in illegal settlements.

Dr Scamps said that the bill seeks to put clear legal “red lines” around Australian involvement in the most serious breaches of international law.

“Despite Australia’s history as a champion of international law, including its commitment to prevent and punish genocide and prohibit torture under international treaties, we are increasingly falling short of these obligations due to critical gaps in our domestic laws,” the Member for Mackellar said.

“In the absence of a Human Rights Act, this package of legislation would ensure that Australia’s policy and actions align with international law and our human rights obligations, ensuring we are on the right side of history.

“This is not about a single country; there are grievous human rights abuses going on in countries all around the world.

“It is not nearly good enough for our government to say they are not sure if components we manufacture here in Australia are being used in F-35s that have killed tens of thousands of people in Gaza.

“There must be no doubt about the integrity of Australian defence supply chains, investments and trade to ensure that everything from local business to the Federal Government is not knowingly or unknowingly complicit in war crimes and genocide and other human rights violations.”

Senator Faruqi, the Greens spokesperson for global justice, said the package was “far from radical” and delivers exactly what Australians expect of their government.

“For three years, Labor has told Australians horrified by the genocide in Gaza that there is nothing our government can do,” she said.

“The Red Lines bill is a comprehensive package of actions the government must take to stop Australia’s complicity in the slaughter and make sure future governments can never go down the same road.”

Without government support, however, the bill has no chance of getting up in the Reps. In the Senate, the crossbench would need to persuade either Labor or the Coalition to get on board.

canberra.title: Teen allegedly leads police on car chase between NSW and ACT
canberra.snippet: Police chased a stolen car from NSW to the ACT and back again before finally getting it to stop and allegedly finding a 16-year-old girl ...
canberra.content:
14 September 2026

14 September 2026

The car chase down the Kings Highway finally ended in Bungendore. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Police chased a stolen car from NSW to the ACT and back again before finally getting it to stop and allegedly finding a 16-year-old girl behind the wheel.

But she is not the only one in trouble, as police have also charged the five young passengers who were allegedly with her in the vehicle.

An NSW Police spokesperson alleged a four-wheel drive was stolen from an address in Canberra on 12 September.

Officers then tried to stop the car for random testing in Queanbeyan, NSW, at around 1:45 am on Monday (14 September).

When the driver allegedly failed to stop, police initiated a pursuit. The pursuit continued through the Queanbeyan CBD, the Kings Highway and into the ACT.

Police began chasing the car again when it reentered NSW. Officers successfully deployed road spikes on the Kings Highway, but the car continued into Bungendore before stopping on Bungendore Road.

The alleged driver and five passengers – identified by police as two 15-year-old boys, a 15-year-old girl and two 16-year-old boys – were all arrested.

The 16-year-old girl police alleged had been driving was handed five charges, including police pursuit, taking and driving a conveyance without consent, and being an unaccompanied learner driver. She was refused bail to appear before a children’s court on Monday.

The five other teenagers were charged with being carried in a conveyance without consent. They were granted bail to face Queanbeyan Local Court in October.

canberra.title: Independent fund proposed to end ‘creative accounting’ club contributions to sporting clubs, reliance on pokies
canberra.snippet: The ACT Greens want to remove any doubt or “creative accounting” around licensed clubs’ community contributions by esta...
canberra.content:
The ACT Greens want to set up an independent fund to manage how licensed clubs’ community contributions are divided up to sports clubs. Photo: ACT Government/Facebook.

The ACT Greens want to remove any doubt or “creative accounting” around licensed clubs’ community contributions by establishing an independent fund for sports groups.

Gambling Harm spokesperson Rebecca Vassarotti will introduce her proposal for an independent Community Contributions Fund, and to mandate clubs pay their entire 8 per cent community contribution in cash rather than in-kind, during the October sitting of the Legislative Assembly.

Her motion will also call for the ACT Government to investigate setting up a compounding investment framework to future-proof local sport funding.

“Local sports shouldn’t have to beg profit-driven clubs for hand-outs, nor should they have to compete in the budget every year,” Ms Vassarotti said.

“By setting up a dedicated fund, with an initial investment base, we could lock in the baseline $6.83 million our sports rely on today, working towards truly independent and self-sustaining sports funding.

“And better yet, this would set the groundwork for clubs to eliminate their reliance on pokies without taking a cent from community sport.”

ACT Greens’ calculations base the $6.83 million on a combination of the current $5.25 million in cash and $1.58 million in non-cash contributions from clubs.

The fund would need an initial $154.07 million contribution, which would earn an assumed 4.43 per cent annual return, to cover the funding that local sports clubs need.

The ACT Greens’ projections for its proposed independent community fund for local sports include the assumption that licensed clubs will contribute $6.83 million in the short term as part of their mandatory contribution obligations. Photo: ACT Greens.

Ms Vassarotti argued the ACT Government needed to remove licensed clubs’ ability to claim that further cuts to poker machines would harm local sports funding options, given the difficulties clubs face in diversifying their profit sources.

“Right now, the big clubs decide where community contributions go with zero strings attached. The cash gets scattered in tiny amounts, diluting its impact and keeping community sport dependent on private businesses,” she said.

“This system, where the government takes a back seat and lets clubs ride roughshod over our community, is fundamentally broken.

“To ensure every dollar actually serves the public, we need to create this independent fund.”

Ms Vassarotti said the second element of the proposal, to mandate the 8 per cent in-kind community contribution from clubs to be cash-only, would close a major loophole in how the system currently worked.

“Last year, Canberra clubs logged nearly $7 million in reported community contributions. But accounting loopholes mean a massive chunk of that is just ‘in-kind’ only, reducing how much real cash gets invested in our community,” she said.

“If we took the actual cash contributions required from clubs, no creative accounting allowed, and put them into an independent central fund, we could better support sports funding as well as better support our community.”

In-kind donations can include things like allowing community groups to use club meeting rooms for free.

According to the ClubsACT frequently asked questions page, Canberra clubs have donated more than $150 million to local sports teams and infrastructure since 2000.

“In the ACT, two-thirds of Canberra’s clubs provide their members with sporting facilities, and collectively there is over $500 million of assets under management. This highlights the importance of clubs in providing the community with sporting and recreational facilities,” it stated.

“Although members pay for the use of these types of sporting facilities, the charges are often below the full cost of provision. The difference, however, is made up from income earned from other parts of clubs’ operation.

“Across clubs at large, the total charges for providing these sporting facilities do not cover the costs of provision.”

ClubsACT has already announced it doesn’t support the proposal in its current form.

CEO Craig Shannon said there was a “legitimate question” about the long-term security of funding as gaming revenue declined, but labelling community contributions as “creative accounting” was “unfair”.

“Clubs already operate under eligibility, reporting and audit requirements. If a particular contribution is overvalued, establish that and correct it. We support defensible valuation standards and proper scrutiny,” he said.

“A free meeting room can be the difference between a volunteer group operating and folding. Access to equipment or a sporting facility can save an organisation money it simply does not have. A service does not become worthless because no cash changes hands.

“Moving recipients from a club relationship into a central grant process also changes who they depend on. It does not, by itself, remove that dependence or make funding more secure.”

Mr Shannon also questioned the financial assumptions, stating they didn’t stack up to secure, ongoing funding.

“The headline calculation uses a 4.43 per cent investment return but separately allows 0.35 per cent for administration and fees. On those assumptions, the initial $154.07 million fund alone would fall approximately $539,000 short of the annual funding target after costs,” he said.

“Subsequent club payments improve the position, but the first-year return after fees still falls approximately $261,000 short of the target, even after the first injection.

“The public deserves a complete model showing who supplies the capital, how grants are paid and who covers shortfalls.”

ClubsACT called for the proposal to be postponed until consultation, an independent financial assessment and a community impact analysis were completed.

canberra.title: Burrito Bar burglar jailed for a string of break-ins across Canberra
canberra.snippet: Cash in strong boxes, tills and even staff pay packets – no money was safe from the prying hands of a serial burglar as he made his...
canberra.content:
One of the many businesses targetted by serial burglar Daniel Robert Weldon was the Burrito Bar in Greenway. Photo: Burrito Bar, Facebook.

Cash in strong boxes, tills and even staff pay packets – no money was safe from the prying hands of a serial burglar as he made his way through Canberra businesses.

Daniel Robert Weldon, 49, was found guilty of two counts of burglary at a judge-alone trial before pleading guilty to 13 more because he said the cases against him were “carrying on too long”, a recently published decision from the ACT Supreme Court says.

Justice Louise Taylor said he and another man first broke into Massage Right in Greenway on 28 September 2022, but couldn’t steal anything because the till was empty.

That same morning, the pair used a crowbar to force their way into the nearby Burrito Bar to steal $500 cash and shattered a glass panel at Elite Supps to steal around $1000 cash.

They travelled to the Kingston Foreshore, where they unsuccessfully tried to break into two businesses before forcing their way into Chong Co Thai Restaurant, where they stole up to $500 cash, and into Walt and Burley, where they stole a laptop and a bottle of rum. The pair also ransacked La Rustica.

Weldon and another man were found guilty of breaking into Brew & Brew in Forrest on 2 October 2022, where they stole a safe and tip jar containing about $7500 cash.

He was also found guilty of breaking into Questacon’s Atomic Cafe, where they stole a safe and money from two tills.

Another 12 burglaries took place in Dickson and Belconnen over 5 to 8 October 2022, when Weldon broke into restaurants, cafes, supermarkets and even the Belconnen Library.

During a burglary spree in Fyshwick over 10 to 14 October 2022, he stole about $1850 during a break-in at KFC Fyshwick, about $3000 cash and $10,000 worth of tobacco pouches and cigarettes from Metro Petrol Station, about $2380 cash from FishCo Fish Market and about $2000 cash from Halal Poultry.

“On any view, the conduct was deliberate and sustained,” Justice Taylor said.

“It was not especially sophisticated; reflected in the lack of ‘success’ as a result of some of the conduct, noting in several instances no items were stolen after the offenders entered the premises.

“The offending comprehends a significant degree of criminality because of the significant number of offences which occurred over a period and the undoubted inconvenience and cost involved to the victims.”

She said Weldon and his co-offender also damaged a couple of stores, including $ 7000 worth of damage to the front door of Metro Petrol.

Weldon was born in Cowra in NSW, has four children and has worked in carpentry, construction and the forestry industry. He suffered traumatic experiences in his life and struggled with drug use.

“[I am] sorry for the losses and disruption that had been experienced by the businesses that had been targeted,” he said.

Justice Taylor said she was satisfied he had shown remorse.

“Plainly the offender’s prospects of rehabilitation are closely connected to his capacity for sobriety,” she said.

“The offender’s drug use as an adult, which was clearly a driver for the offending, is tightly intertwined with his profoundly disadvantaged childhood.”

Weldon spent 371 days in custody before his sentencing. He was convicted and sentenced to about eight years and one month in jail, with a three-year and three-month non-parole period. This means he can be released from December 2028.

canberra.title: Wendy Teakel and Al Munro: life in a local paddock v the glitter of Barcelona
canberra.snippet: Wendy Teakel and Al Munro are two artists who seek inspiration from the domestic to the exotic. Teakel and Munro are veterans of the Canb...
canberra.content:
14 September 2026

Start the conversation

Al Munro, After Barcelona, 2026, acrylic gouache on 54 constructed cardboard forms, overall dimensions 130 x 315 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

Wendy Teakel and Al Munro are two artists who seek inspiration from the domestic to the exotic.

Teakel and Munro are veterans of the Canberra art scene, who are now sharing an exhibition space in Civic. Both artists have developed what might be called a recognisable signature style, which this exhibition pushes a little further.

Teakel has lived in Murrumbateman for many years, where she experiences a rural lifestyle first-hand and the changing seasons and paddock life play an active role in her art-making.

Teakel acknowledges the impact of the American feminist philosopher Donna Haraway, best remembered for her concept of the Cyborg as a metaphor for a hybrid of human, machine, nature and technology.

In other words, she advocates breaking down the classic distinctions between human and animal, nature and culture and body and technology.

Her Cyborg Manifesto (1985) and Staying with the Trouble (2016) elaborate on the idea that humans, animals, technologies and nature are deeply interconnected, leading to a messy, entangled world.

Wendy Teakel, Before Rain, 2026, acrylic, charcoal, pastel, gouache, scorch marks on 640 gsm Arches paper on birch panel, 60 x 60 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

Teakel’s exhibition builds on this idea of entanglement. The artist does not see herself as separate from nature, or as an observer, but as a participant interwoven into a complex, messy, unplanned coexistence.

In pieces such as Before Rain, Full Moon and Grass Matrix, she employs both conventional art materials, including acrylic paint, pastel, gouache and charcoal, and less conventional materials, including soot, scorch marks and pokerwork.

Wendy Teakel, Full Moon, 2026, acrylic, pastel, graphite, gouache, scorch marks on 640 gsm Arches paper on birch panel, 60 x 60 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

She also abandons traditional perspectival structures, as if reckoning that each participant element in her design brings its own perspective, separate and different from the others. She presents an entangled world to the viewer.

Wendy Teakel, Grass Matrix, 2026, soot, charcoal, gouache on 640 gsm Arches paper on birch panel, 30 x 30 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

In some of her more complex pieces, including Earth Carpet and her various quilt and patchwork pieces, there is an attempt, which is not always successful, to bring together this riot of complex and clashing forms with their different forms of visualisation.

It is an ambitious exhibition of the complex, entangled environment the artist inhabits.

Wendy Teakel, Earth Carpet, 2026, acrylic, charcoal, pastel, graphite, pokerwork on 640 gsm Arches paper on birch panel, 152 x 101 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

Al Munro has for many years been exploring patterns, colour and geometry largely as encountered in built urban environments. They are sometimes enormously intricate constructions and stem from the artist’s encounters with various architectural forms.

Recently, Munro spent time living in Barcelona, where, as with most people who visit the great Catalan city, she was blown away by the architectural presence of Antoni Gaudí, especially La Sagrada Família. Her exhibition has arisen in part as a response to the architecture of Lluís Domènech i Montaner and Gaudí as encountered in Barcelona.

Physically, her major installation piece, After Barcelona, and smaller pieces such as Gracia 1 and Gracia 3, consist of acrylic paint on cardboard forms. Although the forms are non-figurative, they are created in response to the encounter with place.

Al Munro, Gracia 1 and Gracia 3, 2026, acrylic paint on constructed cardboard form, 91 x 20 x 6 cm each. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

The artist notes, “As with previous bodies of work, I am interested in exploring the intersection of pattern, colour, geometry and space in painting. Through the construction of shaped and ‘folded’ painting surfaces I seek to disturb and activate the space of the picture plane and create an experience for the viewer which is more dynamic than viewing a 2D painting.”

The exhibition features a proliferation of curved geometry and colour combinations inspired by Barcelona’s architecture, which become quite mesmerising in many of the pieces. Munro’s play with tonal structures of colour is quite marked in many of the pieces.

While both established artists have well-known strategies in their art, this exhibition marks a new page in their work.

Al Munro, After Barcelona, 2026, detail, acrylic gouache on 54 constructed cardboard forms, overall dimensions 130 x 315 cm. Photo: Civic Art Bureau.

Wendy Teakel: Entanglement, and Al Munro: After Barcelona, are at the Civic Art Bureau, Melbourne Building, Level 1, 76 Alinga Street, Civic. It’s open Thursday to Saturday from 12 noon to 5 pm, on Sunday 2 pm to 5 pm. It closes on 4 October.

australia.title: Queen’s secret Whitlam correspondence inspires Sydney Theatre Company play in 2027
australia.snippet: STC’s 2027 program also features Celeste Barber in Amy Sedaris and David Sedaris play, Tim Minchin as Scrooge and the return of The Pictu...
australia.content:
Six years after the Australian historian Jenny Hocking won her legal battle to release secret correspondence between Queen Elizabeth II, Malcolm Fraser and the governor general John Kerr, her fight to reveal the truth about Gough Whitlam’s dismissal is being adapted for the stage.

The Palace Letters, announced on Monday as part of Sydney Theatre Company’s 2027 program, will have its world premiere at Sydney Opera House in April. It will star Georgie Parker as Hocking, with Jonathan Biggins playing Whitlam.

STC’s artistic director, Mitchell Butel, described the play as Hocking’s “Erin Brockovich journey through the court system”, with the first half following the historian’s case and the second taking place immediately after the dismissal.

All together, the STC’s 2027 program boasts four world premieres and six Australian premieres, including Robert Icke’s modern retelling of Oedipus, which starred Lesley Manville and Mark Strong in the West End and Broadway productions. “It’s one of the most electric pieces of theatre I’ve seen,” said Butel, who has cast Heather Mitchell and Richard Roxburgh as Jocasta and Oedipus.

The adaptation takes the Sophocles tragedy and propels it into a contemporary setting, where Oedipus is a politician awaiting election results. It will be staged at Roslyn Packer Theatre in January and February before heading to Adelaide festival in March.

The comedian Celeste Barber will make her STC debut in The Book of Liz, a 90-minute off-Broadway comedy written by the sibling duo David and Amy Sedaris. Barber will play Sister Elizabeth Donderstock, a runaway from a religious sect who is “clueless about sex and the modern world but armed with a formidably sunny disposition”.

STC’s global hit The Picture of Dorian Gray will return to Roslyn Packer Theatre, with the former artistic director Kip Williams back in the director’s chair. Nikki Shiels, who was the understudy for the original Dorian, Eryn Jean Norvill, will step into the spotlight for its homecoming run, playing all 26 characters in the marathon cinetheatre show, which will also tour to Brisbane.

Norvill is also making her return to STC, this time playing all the characters in Vanya – the Olivier award-winning adaptation of Chekhov’s Uncle Vanya. The actor will co-direct the play with Helpmann award-winning director Marion Potts.

Tim Minchin – last seen on stage for STC in 2013’s Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead – is taking on the role of Scrooge in the British playwright Jack Thorne’s adaptation of A Christmas Carol. Matthew Warchus, the British director of Minchin’s hit Matilda the Musical, will direct the Sydney show, which runs from November to Boxing Day.

A brand-new stage version of Miss Fisher’s Murder Mysteries is also on the bill, with Mama Does Derby’s Amber McMahon donning a black bob to play Phryne Fisher. The play takes place on a cruise ship and is adapted from one of Kerry Greenwood’s books which didn’t make it into the Essie Davis TV series. The show premiere will in Brisbane before making its way to Sydney in May.

Also on the program is a new Australian version of the Broadway hit John Proctor is the Villain, about a class of high school students grappling with Arthur Miller’s The Crucible, heading to both Sydney and Melbourne. Becky Shaw, a “cracking dark American comedy about dating and sex and romance and family” straight from Broadway, is also on the cards, as is a Thelma and Louise-style story called Amah and Nanna, starring Home and Away’s Lynne McGranger.

Rounding out the program is “a study of masculinity that isn’t toxic”, Butel said: The Fifth Step, a two-hander starring Ashan Kumar and Erik Thomson as a young man and his AA sponsor. The play, by the Northern Irish-playwright David Ireland, was performed by Martin Freeman and Jack Lowden in London last year.

The Bookbinder of Jericho by Pip Williams, a co-production between STC and State Theatre Company South Australia, will also head to Sydney and Adelaide. And Logan St, written and directed by Jacob Boehme, about friendship found in the grounds of Australia’s oldest mosque, comes to Sydney after its debut in Adelaide this year.

“I genuinely think this is a season that will dazzle on a sensual level,” Butel said. But I really hope the themes speak to who we are as a species and as a nation now.”

australia.title: Indonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicide
australia.snippet: Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own lif...
australia.content:
Indonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life.

The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning.

According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach.

Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement.

The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.

“Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read.

“From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.”

The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling.

The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident.

“Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said.

Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate.

A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians.

“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement.

australia.title: One Nation’s plan to cut migration by 750,000 would ‘smash economy’ and force hospitals to close, Labor says
australia.snippet: Universities Australia says party can’t take skills and jobs out of the country and ‘pretend there will be no consequences’ Follow our Au...
australia.content:
One Nation’s latest immigration policy would “smash the Australian economy” and force hospitals and aged care facilities to close, Labor has warned, while the university sector has urged against a “race to the bottom” on cutting overseas arrivals.

One Nation said on Monday it would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants.

The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, claimed the new policy would “reset” Australia’s immigration system and help ease pressure on housing and public services.

Temporary visa numbers would be returned to 2017 levels, under what Hanson says would represent a net-negative arrivals rate for the first three years. That would mean the net overseas migration (Nom) total would be 130,000 under the One Nation plan.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said a halt on immigration “would smash the Australian economy” and warned regional communities would be the first to suffer.

“Hospitals and aged care facilities would be forced to close,” he said.

“There’d be a chronic shortage of backpackers to work in hospitality and tourism, or to help farmers pick their crops.

“The construction sector would grind to a halt. Regional universities would have to radically shrink or go broke.”

Burke said Hanson should be honest and upfront with Australians about the effect of the new policy.

Luke Sheehy, the chief executive of peak body Universities Australia, said the plan would do lasting damage. He said One Nation was joining Labor and the Coalition in a “race to the bottom” with plans to dramatically cut student visas.

“You can’t take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences,” he said.

“International education is one of Australia’s biggest exports. It supports jobs across the economy, helps build the skilled workforce we desperately need and strengthens our relationships around the world.

“It also helps keep our universities going.”

Immigration debate

Hanson’s announcement comes as Labor and the Coalition consider new cuts to overseas arrivals, in an increasingly charged contest before the next federal election. Hanson will hope her plan plays well in the lead-up to the Victorian state election, due in November.

“I know Australians are doing it tough,” Hanson said. “Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation. Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up.”

The target is to reduce student visa numbers, including visas for accompanying family members, to 350,000 over three years. According to education department data, about 680,000 international students studied in Australia between January to May this year.

A single student graduate program visa will be created, with numbers capped at 20,000 new visas per year. One Nation’s target is to reduce graduate visa numbers from 270,000 to 40,000.

The policy could also drive division within One Nation, with the lower house MP David Farley previously expressing concern that big cuts to immigration could deny his electorate of Farrer the workers needed to care for elderly people and work on farms.

Hanson said One Nation would give “illegal migrants” three months to leave, with those who departed voluntarily allowed to apply for visas in the future.

“Those who remain unlawfully after this period will be subject to immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia,” she said.

The Pacific labour mobility scheme for agriculture would remain in place under One Nation’s plan but temporary skilled migrants would lose the ability to apply for visas for family members.

“We will take back control of who comes here and how many we accept, train more Australians, restore living standards and put the safety and security of Australians first.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, have held talks on Labor’s delayed migration package. It is expected to further drive down net overseas migration.

But Labor has struggled to finalise the plan and delayed its announcement by more than a month.

Australian businesses ‘at risk’

One Nation’s policy was widely criticised by business groups.

Business Council of Australia boss, Bran Black, warned One Nation that migrants were needed for growth in the economy.

“The starting point for any conversation with respect to migration cannot simply have the objective of cutting numbers, it has to be: how do we go about delivering the growth that ultimately locks in and secures our way of life?” he said.

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive, Andrew McKellar, said the business community would not support damaging cuts.

“Many Australian businesses would be put at risk by major cuts to the migration program. Pubs, cafes, hotels and accommodation providers desperately need chefs.

“Aged care homes and hospitals are short of staff already. Farmers and resources sector businesses continue to face persistent workforce shortages. Housing projects are being held up, while others remain unviable because of lack of workforce and skills shortages.”

National Farmers’ Federation boss, Hamish McIntyre, warned food prices could rise due to worker shortages.

“One in seven employees on our farms across regional Australia now are working holidaymakers or backpackers,” he told Channel Nine.

“We need these people now.

“It’ll prohibit us from planting some of these crops. We rely on these people. We won’t be able to take the risks to spend all the money, we spend up front obviously to produce these crops, so we’re not going to take a risk if we can’t harvest them.”

Taylor dismissed the policy as “absolute nonsense”.

“I’m interested to know the details of One Nation’s plan. I don’t know what their non-numbers were. A few days ago, their immigration numbers were 130,000. Now it’s something different. Well, what is it, each year over the next three or four years?

“What are those numbers? They’re not in their releases. They need to explain it.”

Jean Nassif says he is not in communication with someone else during Icac evidence

The NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny has now concluded for this afternoon. Jean Nassif, who has told the commission he has to attend a meeting in Beirut this morning local time, will return to give evidence at 2pm tomorrow afternoon.

Earlier counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked Nassif if he had a phone with him in the room while he is giving evidence. After he said yes, she asked him if he was in communication with anyone, to which he insisted he was not.

Dwyer asked him if he has been in contact with former Toplace executive and lawyer Sharangan Maheswaran, who is named in a separate Icac allegation, and has previously denied any wrongdoing. Nassif was asked earlier if he was reading from a document while giving evidence. He said:

No, I don’t have any document because … the police raided my home, my offices, and … took all the evidence.

Alcohol taxes and marketing need review, inquiry finds

Melissa Davey

A parliamentary inquiry into the health impacts of alcohol and drugs has tabled its final report, recommending new mandatory alcohol advertising and marketing regulations be developed along with national standards for the online sale and delivery of alcohol.

The way alcohol is taxed should also be reviewed, the inquiry recommended, with many of the health groups giving evidence to the inquiry that a uniform volumetric tax across all alcohol products is needed.

Spirits, pre-mixed drinks and beer are currently taxed volumetrically with the amount of tax paid determined by the volume of alcohol within the product. Wine and cider are taxed based on their wholesale price, rather than alcohol content, leading to cheap wine with high alcohol content.

Many previous government reviews have recommended a volumetric tax for wine.

Ayla Chorley, the CEO of the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education, said the recommendations “provide a clear pathway to reduce alcohol-related harm”. She said:

This harm is not inevitable.

The way alcohol is marketed and sold should be determined by governments, not the industry that profits from a harmful and addictive product.

Dr Erin Lalor, the CEO of the Alcohol and Drug Foundation, said the report was a milestone. She said:

This report highlights the significant harms associated with alcohol and other drug use, including long term chronic health conditions, relationship breakdowns and violence against women and children.

One Nation migration plan would badly damage international education, universities warn

Universities Australia has accused One Nation of threatening to destroy “one of Australia’s biggest exports”, warning that “slashing international student numbers would do lasting damage”.

The comments follow Pauline Hanson’s announcement of the party’s immigration policy, which would cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years. The plan targets international students and family members of skilled migrants in a “net-negative” migration policy.

Universities Australia’s chief executive, Luke Sheehy, said the major political parties were competing in “a race to the bottom on international students”. In a statement, he said:

A vote for dramatically fewer international students is a vote for a poorer, less skilled Australia. You can’t take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences.

International education is one of Australia’s biggest exports. It supports jobs across the economy, helps build the skilled workforce we desperately need and strengthens our relationships around the world.

It also helps keep our universities going. For years, governments have asked universities to do more while public funding has failed to keep pace with the cost of teaching, research and infrastructure. International education has helped fill that gap.

If politicians want to rip that revenue out of the system, they need to tell Australians what replaces it.

Read the full story here:

‘Four policies in four weeks’: Canavan questions detail of One Nation’s latest immigration policy

The Nationals leader. Matt Canavan. has questioned the detail and viability of One Nation’s latest immigration policy, saying the party has failed to provide clear costings or explain how its proposed migration cuts would affect key industries.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Canavan said:

It’s a bit hard to judge this policy. It’s the fourth migration policy One Nation has had in four weeks, and still we don’t really see proper costings. There’s no indication of exactly what the numbers would be, that 750,000 figure is over three years.

That’s really important. Those details are really important to industries like farming. There is no doubt we need to get migration numbers down, a lot lower than what the government has them at the moment or even what they want to get them to.

There is a reason One Nation has had four policies in four weeks. They have gone off half-cocked a number of times; they haven’t quite understood the complexities of the system.

Industry and innovation minister Tim Ayres has accused the Coalition of trying to politicise the collapse of the Whyalla steelworks while hundreds of workers face losing their jobs.

The comments came after several Coalition MPs, including shadow industry minister Andrew Hastie, blamed the development on the government’s clean energy transition policies.

Speaking to reporters in Canberra, Senator Ayres said:

After their fellow Australians in Whyalla, people who don’t just put on high-vis shirts for press conferences but put them on everyday and turn up before these guys have even got out of bed and work hard to secure the future of the blast furnace … Mr Hastie, Mr Fanning and Senator Canavan came here and said that this was all about energy costs and net zero. I mean, that is a lie.

It’s trying to politicise the effort and struggle of ordinary Australians in manufacturing who are doing their very best – working together with unions, the business, the administrator, the governments, the joint taskforce.

Everybody is throwing themselves at this giant task, and all these guys can do is turn up and try to use them as political pawns in some contest between One Nation, the Nationals and the Liberals.

Federal government announces $10m dollar support package for Whyalla workers

The federal government has announced a $10m joint support package for the 500 Whyalla workers who face losing their jobs, their families and the broader community affected by the decision to abandon efforts to restart the plant’s troubled blast furnace.

The package will provide career support, transition assistance, skills recognition and funding for workers who want to upgrade or expand their skills. Wellbeing services and financial counselling will also be available.

Speaking in Canberra, employment and workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth said that while it was “a very difficult day”, the decision was not unexpected and support measures had been planned.

The Peter Malinauskas and the Albanese Labor government have been working to plan for the event if this was to occur, so we’ve been able to immediately stand up worker support.

This package has been thought through and will provide support to those workers and, importantly, their families, because we know that these workers are not the only ones affected.

Importantly, we will be working with the South Australian government to ensure that workers who are affected and will no longer have work as a result of this closure get other job opportunities.

Australia records first bird flu case in pelican

Australia has recorded its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a pelican, South Australian authorities have confirmed.

The pelican was found at Edithburgh on the Yorke Peninsula, one of five detection events included on Monday in the state’s latest testing update.

It comes after South Australia recorded the first bird flu death of an endangered Australian sea lion on Sunday.

On Sunday, the state’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said the sea lion was found dead at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island, Australia’s third-largest colony of the animals.

As of the latest federal figures, Australia has recorded more than 500 confirmed events of H5 bird flu in more than 30 species of wildlife, the vast majority of cases in greater crested terns, a common native seabird. South Australia accounts for nearly 300 cases.
